paras: The lynching of William Williams was the killing of a Black farm hand by a mob near Whigham, Decatur County, Georgia, on September 26, 1903. Williams was accused of attacking the seven-year-old daughter of his former employer that morning, and that day a mob of about seventy-five men took him from the men holding him and hanged and shot him. A coroner's jury found no evidence against any member of the mob. Early reports stressed that Whigham residents would give no names or particulars, and the story ran across the country only as a brief wire item.

According to an account in the Savannah Morning News four days later, Williams had worked on the place of a Mr. Harrell, four miles north of Whigham, and was discharged on the morning of Saturday, September 26. A Bainbridge dispatch described him as a farm hand "well known in that section."

The Savannah account said Harrell's daughter was playing in the lot some distance from the house at about 8 o'clock that morning when Williams attacked her, and that her screams brought help from the house and he fled. The first reports described the charge differently: the Bainbridge dispatch called it an "attempted criminal assault," the Thomasville wire said he "assaulted a small white girl," and one digest said he was lynched "for raping" her.

A small posse under the girl's uncle caught Williams soon afterward and, expecting an attempt to lynch him, kept him hidden in the woods, planning to slip him to the jail at Bainbridge after dark. At about 8 o'clock that night, within a mile of Whigham, Harrell and one other guard were met by "a mob of some seventy-five men," which took the prisoner from them. Williams was hanged from a tree and his body was riddled with bullets.

Sheriff Fordham of Bainbridge learned of the lynching by telegram from Whigham and was to leave for the scene on the first train. A coroner's jury, with Postmaster Quinn of Whigham as foreman, held an inquest over the body and found no evidence against any man in the mob, whose ranks the Savannah correspondent thought "must have been filled from people out in the country." No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial was found.

The Savannah Morning News ran the Bainbridge dispatch on September 27 under the headlines "BRUTE PAID PENALTY" and "NEGRO WHO COMMITTED RAPE LYNCHED AT WHIGHAM," although its text spoke of an attempted assault. Beside it the paper printed a Thomasville dispatch headed "Citizens Won't Tell," which reported that telephone and telegraph messages to Whigham drew nothing beyond the fact of the lynching. On September 30 the same paper published the particulars that had "at length leaked out" under the headline "WAS HANGED AND RIDDLED," calling the lynching "the unfortunate affair."

Outside Georgia the story traveled as a short Thomasville wire item, which the Birmingham Age-Herald headed "NEGRO PAYS THE PENALTY" on September 27 and which the Wichita Daily Eagle, Indianapolis Journal, Montgomery Advertiser and St. Paul Globe ran the same day. The Atlanta Constitution printed the Thomasville special on September 28, and the Barre Daily Times in Vermont headed the item "Lynched For the Usual Crime." Weekly news digests repeated it into October, several spelling the town "Wigham," while the Newberry Herald and News said the man was lynched "for the usual crime." Some digests misplaced the lynching at Thomasville, the dateline of the wire.

The only Black-press item found was one line in the Richmond Planet's weekly news summary of October 3, repeating the digest wording that placed the lynching at Thomasville. No Black-press editorial comment on the Whigham lynching was found, and no paper in either press named the girl or reported Williams's own account.

Reports disagreed on the place: the Thomasville wire put the lynching about five miles north of Whigham, while the Bainbridge dispatch and the later Savannah account put it about a mile from the town, the latter placing the Harrell home four miles north. They also differed on the time, the wire saying the afternoon and the Savannah follow-up about 8 o'clock at night; the follow-up, written after the inquest, is the more detailed account.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed the first report 'BRUTE PAID PENALTY' and 'FIEND FORFEITED HIS LIFE SIX HOURS AFTER CRIME', and the Birmingham Age-Herald 'NEGRO PAYS THE PENALTY'.
The Savannah follow-up called it 'the unfortunate affair' and noted that no evidence was found against the mob.
Papers outside Georgia ran the Thomasville wire as a brief, some headed or phrased 'for the usual crime'.
The Richmond Planet carried only the wire digest line, without comment.
